source_law: AI proposes. Policy authorizes. CI proves. The human promotes.

intent.goal: Give LuHm Python 3 the shortened intent-first feel the Professor likes in jQuery while preserving explicit architecture and boring-safe internals.
intent.surface_rule: Short on the surface, boring underneath.
intent.migration_rule: Add wrappers and contracts first. Move old code only after tests prove the wrapper path.

plugin.meaning: Explicitly registered optional capability with metadata, defaults, lifecycle, validation and public methods.

class.meaning: Stateful object model for behavior, composition and stable extension boundaries.

python_architecture.json_boundary: DECODE -> VALIDATE -> TYPED PYTHON -> OPERATE -> ENCODE

vowel_rip_human_naming.rule: Derive artifact identifiers from the human phrase by removing a, e, i, o and u while preserving consonant order, then remove spaces and punctuation.

tone_examples: Keeps the weird little optional demons in labeled jars.
If this starts importing half the cathedral, we have failed.
Incoming JSON enters here wearing a fake mustache. Validate it before letting it near anything expensive.
OLD DRAGON CAVE: kept temporarily because ancient imports still live here. Do not build condos.

implementation_order: Define the public library/plugin/class contracts and stubs.
Wrap existing implementation behind the new contracts without moving it.
Migrate one implementation organ at a time only after wrapper evidence is GREEN.
Retire compatibility paths only after no active import depends on them.
hard_laws: Compact syntax must not erase architecture.
Library, plugin and class are different concepts and remain visibly different in the public API.
Vowel-ripped identifiers retain an adjacent human-readable phrase where practical.
Breadcrumb remarks explain intent and boundaries, not obvious syntax.
Humor may decorate truth but may not obscure danger, authority or failure.
AI-generated provider text never gains automatic execution authority.

seal.meaning: This crown governs future LuHm Python organization and coding breadcrumbs. It does not claim that existing Python has already been migrated or tested under the new structure.
